title_en: There's a Mind-Boggling Number of Rich People in America
title_zh: 美国的百万富翁多到令人咋舌：Owen Zidar 与 Eric Zwick 谈穿透式企业与富人
subtitle_zh: 两位经济学家用 IRS 数据揭示，美国真正的富人藏在汽车经销、啤酒分销等穿透式小企业背后。
description: There's a Mind-Boggling Number of Rich People in America

turns.en: Bloomberg Audio Studios. Podcasts. Radio.
turns.zh: Bloomberg Audio Studios。播客。广播。

turns.en: News.
turns.zh: 新闻。

turns.en: Hello and welcome to another episode of the All Thoughts Podcast. I'm Tracy Allaway.
turns.zh: 大家好，欢迎收听新一期的 Odd Lots。我是 Tracy Alloway。

turns.en: And I'm Joe Weisenthal.
turns.zh: 我是 Joe Weisenthal。

turns.en: Joe, I have a very exciting episode for you today.
turns.zh: Joe，今天我给你准备了一期特别精彩的节目。

turns.en: Go on.
turns.zh: 说来听听。

turns.en: We are going to be talking about pass-throughs, S-cores, and the U.S. tax code.
turns.zh: 我们要聊的是穿透式实体（pass-throughs）、S 型公司（S-corps），还有美国税法（U.S. tax code）。

turns.en: This is so great. I'm so excited about this because I remember during some of those tax cut negotiations and you'd have, who is that? I think it was a senator from Wisconsin, Ron Johnson. And he was like, or I don't know which one it was, but he was like, oh, we really need to preserve some pass-through. And I didn't learn about it. And then I was like, well, you know, whatever. And then I missed it. And I was like, great. So finally here in 2026, I can learn about something that I really should have learned earlier. in December of 2017.
turns.zh: 这太棒了。我特别期待，因为我记得在那几轮减税谈判的时候，会有人说——是谁来着？我记得是威斯康星州的一位参议员，Ron Johnson。他当时说，哦，我们真的得保留一些穿透式优惠（pass-through）。我当时没搞懂，然后就想，管它呢，然后就错过了。所以终于在 2026 年，我能补上这门我早在 2017 年 12 月就该学会的课了。

turns.en: Well, actually, I'm glad you said that because this is sort of the thrust of what this entire conversation is going to be, which is when we talk about tax breaks for the wealthy, we normally talk about or we think about Jeff Bezos paying like zero percent income tax or something like that. But actually, a lot of the tax cuts that we've seen, I guess, since the 1980s and now most recently under the Trump administration are have been for S-cores, for these pass-through entities, which generally get framed as small businesses.
turns.zh: 其实我很高兴你提到这个，因为这差不多就是我们整场对话要讲的核心。就是说，当我们谈到给富人的税收优惠时，我们通常想到的、或者说脑子里想到的是 Jeff Bezos 缴纳大约百分之零的所得税之类的。但实际上，我们看到很多的减税——我想是从 1980 年代开始，最近又是在 Trump 政府下——都是针对 S 型公司、针对这些穿透式实体的，而它们通常被包装成小企业。

turns.en: That's right.
turns.zh: 没错。

turns.en: But as it turns out, a lot of these businesses are actually phenomenally large and very, very wealthy.
turns.zh: 但事实证明，这些企业里有很多其实规模惊人地大，而且非常非常有钱。

turns.en: Yeah, there's a few things that I think are really interesting here. So, obviously, people just, like, love the sound of small business, right? Like, small business makes people feel good, whatever it is. People, like, it's sort of something aesthetically interesting.
turns.zh: 对，我觉得这里有几点特别有意思。首先，显然大家就是喜欢‘小企业’这个说法，对吧？小企业让人感觉良好，不管是什么。大家就是……它在某种审美上很有吸引力。

turns.en: Something very American as well. You think about Tocqueville and his big impression of America was, oh, it's this nation of entrepreneurs.
turns.zh: 也很有美国味。你会想到 Tocqueville，他对美国的深刻印象就是，哦，这是一个由创业者组成的国家。

turns.en: Yeah. So there's something about small business that feels good, etc. The other thing that I'm really interested in, and I brought this up a couple of times on the podcast, you know, I think when a lot of people think about the United States or the American economy and the sort of distribution of wealth and income and so forth, there is an incredible, you know, people talk about inequality and then they think, okay, there's like a 1% or a 0.1% that's insanely wealthy. You mentioned Jeff Bezos and a handful of others like that. And then people are aware of the fact that for a country as rich as ours, there's probably unacceptably high levels of like poverty and people perceive there correctly to be a lot of people who are financially struggling, et cetera. But I always think that like the missing thing is like that fat layer of rich people. And the thing that I'm always reminded by it, you know, we're recording this September 9th. I think by the time people listen to this, we'll have already been there. But whenever we go to Southern California, Orange County, Huntington Beach.
turns.zh: 对。所以小企业身上有种让人感觉良好的东西，等等。另一件我特别感兴趣的——我在播客里提过好几次——你知道，我觉得很多人想到美国或者美国经济、想到财富和收入的分配等等时，会有个令人难以置信的……大家谈论不平等，然后想，好吧，有个 1% 或者 0.1% 的人富得离谱。你提到 Jeff Bezos 和少数几个那样的人。然后大家也意识到，对一个像我们这么富裕的国家来说，贫困水平可能高得让人无法接受，人们也正确地感觉到有很多人在经济上挣扎，等等。但我总觉得缺失的那一块，是那厚厚一层的富人。让我一直想起这个——你知道，我们是 9 月 9 日录的这期。我想等大家听到的时候，我们应该已经去过了。但每当我们去南加州、Orange County、Huntington Beach 的时候……

turns.en: And you just see like all these people with boats and you see all these people, you go to like a steakhouse or something and they have their own private like wine locker at the steakhouse.
turns.zh: 你就会看到一大堆有游艇的人，你去个牛排馆之类的，他们在那儿都有自己的私人酒柜。

turns.en: And it's like.
turns.zh: 就是说。

turns.en: There's a lot of rich people.
turns.zh: 那儿有很多富人。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.en: And they're not all like the tech billionaires.
turns.zh: 而且他们并不都是那种科技亿万富翁。

turns.en: They're not all on the Forbes 400 or whatever.
turns.zh: 也不都在 Forbes 400 榜单上什么的。

turns.en: We have a big, fat layer of like just really rich people. And they're not people who made some great invention, et cetera, necessarily, or some Great, huge breakthrough. But like whether it's like real estate or cars or just some sort of simple business, a lot of really rich people in this country.
turns.zh: 我们有厚厚一大层就是非常非常有钱的人。而且他们不一定是靠什么伟大发明之类发家的，或者什么重大的突破。但不管是房地产、汽车，还是某种简单的生意，这个国家有非常多真正的富人。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.en: And we should talk about them, try to figure out who they are, how many of them there actually are. And the one other thing I would also add that makes this sort of a very oddlotsy episode is we talk a lot about.
turns.zh: 我们应该聊聊他们，弄清楚他们是谁、到底有多少人。我还想补充一点，让这一期特别有 Odd Lots 味道的是，我们经常聊……

turns.en: The private markets, right?
turns.zh: 私募市场（private markets），对吧？

turns.en: Private credit, private markets, private equity.
turns.zh: 私募信贷（private credit）、私募市场、私募股权（private equity）。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.en: And often when we are talking about those specific businesses, we are talking about these types of businesses. So, you know, a private equity firm, you think of it as this Wall Street entity, but it owns a portfolio of, I don't know, HVAC companies in Missouri or something.
turns.zh: 而当我们谈论那些具体的生意时，我们说的往往就是这类企业。所以你知道，一家私募股权公司，你会把它想成华尔街的实体，但它拥有一整个投资组合，比如，我不知道，Missouri 州的一堆暖通空调（HVAC）公司什么的。

turns.en: And the last thing I'll say, and I don't know how much we'll get into this part per se. But if you think about, I don't know, the dark matter of American politics, et cetera, privately owned companies are often, or the owners of privately owned companies some regional beverage distributor or something like that, are often very important figures in regional politics. And senators, if you want to get your handle on that, should sort of know who these people are and how they got there.
turns.zh: 我最后要说的一点是——我不知道我们会具体聊到多少这部分——但如果你想，比如美国政治里的‘暗物质’（dark matter）之类的，私有企业，或者说私有企业的所有者，比如某个区域性的饮料分销商之类的，往往是地方政治里非常重要的人物。而参议员们，如果你想搞清楚那套东西，就应该知道这些人是谁、他们是怎么走到今天的。

turns.en: We'll get into that, definitely. So I'm happy to say we do, in fact, have the perfect guest. We're going to be speaking with the authors of the new book, The Everywhere Millionaire, who is really rich in America and how they got there. And the authors are Owen Zadar, professor of economics at Princeton, and Eric Zwick, Professor of Economics and Finance at Chicago Booth. So thank you both so much for being here.
turns.zh: 我们肯定会聊到。所以我很高兴地说，我们确实请到了完美的嘉宾。我们要和新书 The Everywhere Millionaire 的作者们聊聊，这本书讲的是‘美国到底谁最有钱、他们是怎么发家的’。作者是 Owen Zidar，Princeton 经济学教授，以及 Eric Zwick，Chicago Booth 经济与金融学教授。非常感谢两位来到这里。

turns.en: Thanks for having us. It's great to be here.
turns.zh: 谢谢你们邀请我们，很高兴来到这里。

turns.en: It's a great book. Legitimately, I really enjoyed it. When I was reading it, I was thinking it's sort of like an upscale Studs Terkel. You have all these stories of millionaires and how they actually got there. But the origin story of this book is something I wanted to ask you about because it also sits squarely within Oblott's territory when we talk about I guess, what a mess government data and technology tends to be. Because this book started with a project, a commission by the Treasury Department to try to sift through IRS data to figure out who these people actually were and how many of them there are. Talk to us about what you found when you started that project.
turns.zh: 这是一本很棒的书。说真的，我读得很开心。读的时候我就想，它有点像高档版的 Studs Terkel。你有这么多百万富翁的故事，讲他们到底是怎么发家的。但这本书的缘起是我想问你们的，因为它也正好落在 Odd Lots 的地盘里——我们聊过，政府的数据和技术往往是一团糟。这本书起步于一个项目，是财政部（Treasury Department）委托的，想从 IRS 的数据里筛查，弄清楚这些人到底是谁、有多少人。跟我们讲讲你们启动那个项目时发现了什么。

turns.en: Yes. So we started more than a decade ago, commissioned by the Treasury to go into the bowels of the Treasury and work with tax data to try and link all the businesses to their owners and workers because they didn't have the ability to do that and they needed it to do tax policy to sort of think about what if we change the tax code, how much tax these pass-through businesses pay. They didn't have the capacity to do that because the data weren't connected. And so that was the original kind of sin of our project. That was the foundation of our project was to sort of build this data that as we continued to expand it, add years, add different types of layers on it by looking at just the entrepreneurs, for instance, we could start to see, oh, there's actually a picture of income, wealth, entrepreneurship, prosperity in the American economy that is very different than the picture that we were getting from the media, the picture we were getting from the capital book and so on. And so that's sort of the beginning was that kind of nerdy tax data project, the computers, the databases, the XML and so on, which we can talk more about, but that's where we started.
turns.zh: 好。所以我们十多年前就开始了，受财政部委托，钻进财政部的老底子里，去处理税务数据，想办法把所有企业和它们的所有者、员工关联起来，因为他们没有这个能力，而做税收政策又需要这个——去想，如果我们改了税法，这些穿透式企业会缴多少税。他们没有这个能力，因为数据之间没有打通。所以我们项目最初的起点就是这个。项目的基础就是搭建这套数据，随着我们不断扩展它、加入年份、加上不同的层次，比如只看那些创业者，我们开始看到，哦，原来美国经济里收入、财富、创业、繁荣的图景，跟我们当时从媒体上、从《Capital》那本书上得到的图景非常不一样。所以这算是个开端，是那种书呆子气的税务数据项目——电脑、数据库、XML 之类的，这些我们可以多聊聊，但那就是我们的起点。

turns.en: Well, I wanted to ask about the databases, actually, because it just sounded like a nightmare the way you described it. And then there's this funny moment in the book where you basically like randomly find the guy who kind of built these systems and understood them and was able to help you wrap your head around them. How difficult was this?
turns.zh: 其实我想问问那些数据库，因为你描述的方式听起来简直是场噩梦。书里还有个很好笑的地方，你们基本上是偶然找到了那个差不多算是搭建了这些系统、也懂这些系统的人，他能帮你们理清头绪。这有多难？

turns.en: I mean, so the underlying data are basically everything on a tax form. So, you know, you can have information about the business. You can have investors in the business who get money going to them. They're not made to be linked, and many of them aren't electronically filed.
turns.zh: 我的意思是，底层数据基本上就是税表上的一切。所以你知道，你可以有关于企业的信息，可以有企业的投资人——钱会流向他们。这些数据本来不是设计来相互关联的，而且很多都不是电子申报的。

turns.en: When you say they're not made to be linked, what's not made?
turns.zh: 你说它们不是设计来关联的，什么东西不是设计来关联的？

turns.en: They're separate databases.
turns.zh: 它们是相互独立的数据库。

turns.en: So they're just different forms. So when you say Joe and Tracy had an S Corp and you own it 50-50, you can file the business's form, and then you have to file an investor form that says, all right, half the profits are going to Joe, half the profits are going to Tracy. And the way they set up the identifiers was, aren't made where you're supposed to be able to add up all the things from investors and that should add up everything from the business. So the story about how we figured out how to do this, we're going through old code books, like things were called different variable names. And Eric, I don't know if you want to tell the story about going to a part of Utah. Yeah.
turns.zh: 所以就是不同的表格。比如说 Joe 和 Tracy 有一家公司是 S 型公司，你俩五五开持有，你可以申报公司的那张表，然后你还得申报一张投资人表，上面写：好，一半利润归 Joe，一半利润归 Tracy。而他们设置这些标识符的方式，本来不是让你能把投资人那边的所有东西加起来、跟企业那边的全部对上的。所以我们搞清楚怎么做的这个过程——我们在翻旧的编码手册（code books），因为很多东西用的是不同的变量名。Eric，我不知道你要不要讲讲去 Utah 某个地方的那个故事。好。

turns.en: So I'm like giving a talk at Utah state. And I knew that one of the guys who designed the XML system that when people electronically file their tax returns, it's sort of like the formula for converting those tax returns into rows and columns that then get processed, lived on the way from the airport to the lecture I was giving. So I was like, can I come and just ask you some questions? And so I met him for lunch.
turns.zh: 我当时在 Utah State 做一场演讲。我知道有一个人，他设计了那套 XML 系统——就是当人们电子申报报税表时，那套把报税表转换成行列、然后被处理的公式——他就住在我从机场去演讲地点的路上。所以我就想，我能不能过去问你几个问题？于是我就跟他一起吃午饭。

turns.en: We had burgers.
turns.zh: 我们吃了汉堡。

turns.en: What were you thinking?
turns.zh: 你当时怎么想的？

turns.en: I was imagining like in the Matrix, you know, like you go see the Oracle and it's like this old lady, you know, who's like the spoon is bending, you know.
turns.zh: 我脑子里想的是《黑客帝国》（the Matrix）里那种，你知道，你去找先知（the Oracle），是这么个老太太，她说‘勺子是在弯曲的’，那种。

turns.en: I was imagining like some guy who like like kind of a hermit. It's like someone knocking on his door, it's like, why are you here? What do you want? And he's like, that's not me. And then finally after, no, but keep going.
turns.zh: 我脑子里想的是某个有点像隐士的家伙。就像有人敲他的门，‘你来这儿干嘛？你想要什么？’他说‘那不是我’。然后最后，‘不不，你接着说’。

turns.en: He was a super reasonable, he was kind of wearing like a flannel shirt as everybody in Utah seems to do. He wanted to have a beer at lunch and I was happy to join him. And I had my like list of 25 questions that are like very intricate questions about the structure of this database. We had to rearrange columns in order to create the links to to match the business forms to the individuals. And we didn't know what any of these columns were necessarily.
turns.zh: 他超级通情达理，穿着件法兰绒衬衫——Utah 的每个人好像都这么穿。他想午饭时喝杯啤酒，我也很乐意陪他。我带了那 25 个问题的清单，都是非常细致的、关于这个数据库结构的问题。我们得重新排列这些列，才能建立起关联，把企业表和个人的信息对上。而我们当时根本不确定这些列都是什么意思。

turns.en: What year is this, by the way? This is like.
turns.zh: 顺便问一下，这是哪一年？这大概是……

turns.en: Okay, great.
turns.zh: 好，太好了。

turns.en: So yeah, so you can't ask Claude to read the manual and read the code. There's no way to do that. There's no documentation. There's just this knowledge in people's brains that you have to find to try and do this link. And there were other people who kind of knew some of these details, but we couldn't really get to the bottom of it until... having a burger and beer with the architect.
turns.zh: 所以，是啊，你没法让 Claude 去读手册、读代码。没办法那么做。根本没有文档。就只有存在人们脑子里的这些知识，你得把它们找出来，才能做这个关联。也有其他人大致知道一些细节，但我们一直没能真正弄清楚底细，直到……跟那位架构师一起吃汉堡、喝啤酒。

turns.en: It's sort of a diversion, but I feel like I've read so many NBER working papers, which include the line, we exploit a novel data set. How much of economics is finding a novel data set? We think of it as like, oh, maybe we're going to apply some econometrics or theory or whatever. How much are just, as professional economists, is it about finding that data?
turns.zh: 这算是扯开话题了，但我觉得我读过太多 NBER 工作论文（working papers），里面都有那句‘我们利用了一个新颖的数据集’。经济学里有多大成分是在于找到一个新颖的数据集？我们会想，哦，也许我们要用点计量经济学或者理论什么的。作为职业经济学家，有多少其实就是在于找到那个数据？

turns.en: I think it's an important part, but it's also, you need to ask an important question. And if you are thinking about how do people get rich, and you only see a small sliver of how it actually works, and then suddenly you can say, You know, there's 1,000 private business owners that have $ 25 million for every large public company CEO. Like, we've missed all of these people. And now, for the first time, you can trace back, like, where did these people come from?
turns.zh: 我觉得这是很重要的一部分，但你还需要问一个重要的问题。如果你在思考人们是怎么变富的，而你只看到它实际运作的一小条缝隙，然后突然你能说，你知道，每一家大型上市公司 CEO 对应着 1,000 个拥有 2,500 万美元的私有企业主。就是说，我们之前完全漏掉了这些人。而现在，第一次，你可以回溯，这些人是从哪儿来的？

turns.en: Like, what are they doing? How did they do it?
turns.zh: 他们在做什么？他们是怎么做到的？

turns.en: That, I think, opens it up and opens up a lot of work, where I think you're right. Like, there's one of Eric's advisors, Andre Schleifer, teaches a class at Harvard, and he basically– gives the college students at the assignment, like, find me a cool data set. And like, that's how you write the paper. It's like, show me something I haven't seen before. So there's certainly something to find a novel thing to get a hook on something we care about. Yeah.
turns.zh: 我觉得这就打开了局面，也打开了大量研究空间，我想你说得对。Eric 的一位导师，Andre Schleifer，在 Harvard 教一门课，他基本上就给本科生布置作业，说，给我找一个酷的数据集。你就是这么写论文的。就是，给我看点我没见过的东西。所以找到一个新颖的东西、给我们关心的议题找到一个切入点，这确实有价值。

turns.en: But figuring out the question to ask with that data is kind of the trick. Like the data is sitting there like, oh, we can use this to understand inequality.
turns.zh: 但搞清楚用这些数据去问什么问题，才是那个窍门。数据就摆在那儿，哦，我们能用它来理解不平等。

turns.en: Okay. Okay.
turns.zh: 好。好。

turns.en: Maybe this is like jumping forward, but just finally relieve me. What is pass-through made? Like, I mean, finally, like, I'm just going to ask it. When we talk about like, oh, this center really wants to preserve or expand a pass-through induction. What are we talking about here?
turns.zh: 也许这有点往后跳了，但总算让我问出来吧。什么是穿透式（pass-through）？我是说，终于，我就直接问了。当我们说，哦，这个……真的很想保留或者扩大穿透式优惠时，我们说的到底是什么？

turns.en: So pass-through businesses are. different than traditional corporations. So if you look at like a typical public company like GM, they're a C corporation. They face the corporate tax. So when they make profits, they have to pay the corporate tax. And then if they want to send money to individual investors, they have to pay dividends. Pass-throughs are a different part of the tax code where you don't have to face the corporate tax, just the profits and losses go directly to the owners. And they weren't that big of a deal in the 80s. The lion's share of profits and activity were in traditional corporations. And then after Reagan cut taxes in 1986 on individuals lower than corporations, that suddenly became the most attractive way to organize yourself. And so we've seen this huge boom in pass-through entities where that's the vast majority of businesses in America and like half of profits.
turns.zh: 穿透式企业和传统公司不一样。所以如果你看一家典型的上市公司，比如 GM，它是 C 型公司（C corporation）。它要面对公司税（corporate tax）。所以它赚了利润，就得缴公司税。然后如果它想把钱分给个人投资者，就得发股息。穿透式则是税法里另一块，你不用面对公司税，利润和亏损直接归到所有者身上。它们在 80 年代还不算什么大事。绝大部分的利润和经济活动都在传统公司里。后来 Reagan 在 1986 年把个人的税率降到比公司还低，那一下子就变成了最有吸引力的组织形式。所以我们看到了穿透式实体的巨大爆发，如今它占了美国企业的绝大多数，还有大约一半的利润。

turns.en: So, OK, once you figured out the IRS code and got the, I guess, IRS servers that seem to be run by hamsters spinning on wheels to actually work, what were your findings about wealth in America?
turns.zh: 那么，好，一旦你们搞懂了 IRS 的代码、让那些看起来像是由仓鼠在轮子上跑来驱动的 IRS 服务器真正运转起来，你们关于美国财富的发现是什么？

turns.en: So this income is among the most concentrated. So pass-through business income, 70% of every dollar pass-through business income goes to the top 1%. And if you look at the rise of income inequality, so like the famous graph, top 1% share of income from Piketty and Saez going back to the 1980s, more than half of the growth from that period of time to the 2021 is coming in the form of pass-through business income. So you want to understand what's driving income inequality and wealth inequality, because it's sort of a parallel story there. You really have to understand this pass-through business sector. What is the nature of this activity? We knew it was pass-through business income. We didn't really know if this is like Monopoly Man, big business, that you're just passively collecting the income, or what we turned out to find, it was sort of these mid-market regional businesses of which there were just millions of them across the country. And that was kind of like the second huge finding about you know, who these pass-through business owners were and what they're doing. Owen, you want to tell them, like, our mnemonic from reading our kids, like, little books?
turns.zh: 这部分收入是最集中的之一。穿透式企业收入，每 1 美元里有 70% 流向了最富的 1%。如果你看收入不平等的上升，就是那张著名的图——Piketty 和 Saez 画的、回溯到 1980 年代的最富 1% 收入份额——从那个时期到 2021 年，超过一半的增长是以穿透式企业收入的形式出现的。所以你想理解是什么在驱动收入不平等和财富不平等，因为那里有个平行的故事，你就真的得理解这个穿透式企业部门。这类活动的本质是什么？我们知道那是穿透式企业收入。但我们并不真的知道这是不是那种‘大富翁先生’（Monopoly Man）式的大企业——你就被动地收着钱——还是……结果我们发现，是这些中端市场的区域性企业，全国范围内有几百万家。这算是关于这些穿透式企业主是谁、在做什么的第二个重大发现。Owen，你要不要跟他们讲讲我们那个从给孩子读的小书里想出来的记忆口诀？

turns.en: Yeah, so I have three young kids. Eric has one young kid.
turns.zh: 好，我有三个小孩，Eric 有一个小孩。

turns.en: And we're half-jokingly thinking about writing a kid's book of the ABCs of getting rich.
turns.zh: 我们半开玩笑地想着写一本儿童书，讲发家致富的 ABC。

turns.en: And we just go through and have a fun fact on each of them.
turns.zh: 我们就一个个过，每个字母配一个有趣的事实。

turns.en: And so A is for auto dealer, B is for beverage distribution business owner, and then C is for contractor owner.
turns.zh: A 是汽车经销商（auto dealer），B 是饮料分销企业主（beverage distribution business owner），然后 C 是承包商所有者（contractor owner）。

turns.en: D is dentist. You know, we could go through. We actually did it. We haven't made the book.
turns.zh: D 是牙医（dentist）。你知道，我们能一路过下去。我们其实真做了。只是还没做成书。

turns.en: You got to do it. Can I just say, my son is obsessed with money. And finally, no, he's like raised.
turns.zh: 你们得做出来。我能说一句吗，我儿子对钱特别着迷。而且，不，他……

turns.en: Shocking. Yeah, where does he get it from?
turns.zh: 太让人震惊了。是啊，他这是随谁呢？

turns.en: I don't know where. No, it's like, he's always scheming. So he would love this book. So please write it.
turns.zh: 我不知道随谁。不，就是，他老在盘算。所以他肯定会喜欢这本书。所以请务必写出来。

turns.en: Okay. P is for podcaster.
turns.zh: 好。P 是播客主（podcaster）。

turns.en: Oh, yeah.
turns.zh: 哦，对。

turns.en: All right.
turns.zh: 好吧。

turns.en: So give us an example that like, let's dive into a specific one. And I'm just going to choose car dealerships because this is an interesting one. I think everyone knows how a car dealership theoretically is supposed to work. And I don't think you normally think of used cars or I shouldn't say used cars, but car dealers as super wealthy. And yet you have a lot of examples in the book of people who have accumulated millions, if not sometimes billions from this business.
turns.zh: 那给我们举个例子吧，我们深入讲一个具体的。我就选汽车经销商（car dealerships），因为这个挺有意思。我想每个人都知道汽车经销商理论上该怎么运作。而且我觉得你通常不会把二手车——或者说我不该说二手车——但不会把汽车经销商想成超级有钱。可你们书里有很多例子，讲有人靠这门生意积累了几百万、有时甚至几十亿。

turns.en: So.
turns.zh: 所以。

turns.en: The book opens with the wedding of the century, which is a wedding, Bob and Paul of Brockway, Coral Gables, Florida. They sent their daughter to first to the Amangiri for the bachelorette party. It was a four-day party where they dressed up like Marie Antoinette. But then they flew all the guests to Paris for a five-day wedding.
turns.zh: 这本书开篇讲的就是那场‘世纪婚礼’（wedding of the century），是 Bob 和 Paul，来自 Florida 州 Coral Gables 的 Brockway 家族。他们先把女儿送到 Amangiri 办单身派对（bachelorette party）。那是个为期四天的派对，他们打扮成 Marie Antoinette 的样子。然后他们把所有宾客飞到 Paris，办了个为期五天的婚礼。

turns.en: On private jets. On jets. They rented.
turns.zh: 坐私人飞机。坐飞机。他们租了……

turns.en: Versailles, not for the wedding, but just for like a dinner. What year are we talking about here?
turns.zh: Versailles——不是为了婚礼，只是为了办一场晚宴。我们说的是哪一年来着？

turns.en: Okay, 24, yeah. This was 2023, 2024, a few years ago, and it was all over social media.
turns.zh: 好，24 年，对。这是 2023、2024 年，几年前，当时在社交媒体上铺天盖地。

turns.en: I remember this.
turns.zh: 我记得这个。

turns.en: The wedding of the century. Adam Levine sang the first dance. You could see the Eiffel Tower illuminated in the distance. And they're car dealers, third-generation car dealers from Florida, the Mercedes dealer. And they had just sold the dealership. Uh, for several hundred million dollars to actually a consortium that Nick Saban was a co-owner of, um, but they dropped $ 60 million on this wedding.
turns.zh: 世纪婚礼。Adam Levine 唱了第一支舞。你能看到远处的 Eiffel Tower 亮着灯。他们是汽车经销商，来自 Florida 的第三代汽车经销商，Mercedes 经销商。他们刚刚把经销权卖掉了，卖了几亿美元，买家其实是一个 Nick Saban 也是共有人的财团。但他们在这场婚礼上砸了 6,000 万美元。

turns.en: Wow.
turns.zh: 哇。

turns.en: And, um, you know, they're not even close to the top of the list in terms of the most prodigious car dealers in the country. So when we like zoom out and look at the industries that generate the most pass through business income and the top 0.1%, the auto dealers were the number one bucket, which we were like, okay, this is not the. Bickety story of like billionaire tech or finance. This is something different. What are these car dealers doing as an example industry? And then we found them even more when we started looking in like yacht and jet registration data. They just own all these yachts and jets. And that's how we found them by name because the tax data that we were talking about before, we couldn't identify people that way. So when we set out to write the book and tell a bunch of stories, okay, let's find other data sources. We know the rough signatures, we know where to look, but let's find the people that by name so we can tell a little bit more of their background, their story.
turns.zh: 而且，你知道，就全国最能赚的汽车经销商而言，他们连榜单顶端都算不上。所以当我们放大视角，去看那些在最富 0.1% 里产生最多穿透式企业收入的行业时，汽车经销商是排第一的类别，我们当时就想，好，这不是那种亿万富翁科技或金融的老套故事。这是不一样的东西。以汽车经销商这个行业为例，他们到底在做什么？然后当我们开始看游艇和私人飞机的注册数据时，我们发现他们更多——他们就是拥有一大堆游艇和飞机。我们就是这样按名字找到他们的，因为之前说的那些税务数据没法那样识别到人。所以当我们着手写这本书、讲一堆故事时，就说，好，我们去找其他数据源。我们知道大致的特征，知道去哪儿找，但要按名字找到这些人，这样才能多讲讲他们的背景、他们的故事。

turns.en: I love that.
turns.zh: 我太喜欢这个了。

turns.en: Looking at yacht registries to find rich people. It makes sense, but I'm guessing not many people have done it before. Yeah.
turns.zh: 看游艇注册记录来找富人。这说得通，但我猜以前没多少人这么做过。对。

turns.en: I'm curious, like from a pure like economics perspective, when we think about, let's say someone's salary, it's like, okay, here's a really talented person. Maybe they're really great with computers. Maybe they have a lovely voice that sounds great on podcasts. And they're like, okay, this is maybe a rare skill, et cetera. So they're going to get a lot of money. Or maybe we think about like someone who makes a great invention or whatever, and everyone wants to buy it and they get a slice of it. And so they make a lot of money. Let's just stick with car dealers, for example. How would you characterize what these very successful car dealers have brought to the table such that the economy has rewarded them with such riches?
turns.zh: 我很好奇，纯粹从经济学角度看，当我们想某个人的薪水时，是这样：好，这是个非常有才华的人。也许他特别擅长电脑，也许她有一副很好听、在播客里很棒的声音。他们就说，好，这也许是一种稀缺技能之类的，所以他们会赚很多钱。或者我们想某个做出伟大发明的人，人人都想买，他从中抽一份，所以赚很多钱。就拿汽车经销商来说吧。你会怎么描述这些非常成功的汽车经销商到底带来了什么，以至于经济给了他们这么多财富作为回报？

turns.en: So that's a great question.
turns.zh: 这是个好问题。

turns.en: I think, let me tell two stories of car dealers that kind of give a flavor of the complexity, even within car dealers. So one of my favorite ones is a story we tell in the book is about Larry Miller. And Larry Miller is from Utah. He basically worked in the parts department at a Toyota and he learned every single, almost like your Aldi guy. He like knew all the parts and he turned it from the 961st best car dealer of parts, of Toyota parts, to the first.
turns.zh: 我想讲两个汽车经销商的故事，能体现出即便是汽车经销商内部也很复杂。我最喜欢的一个，是我们在书里讲的 Larry Miller 的故事。Larry Miller 来自 Utah。他基本上是在一家 Toyota 的零件部门干活，他学会了每一个零件，几乎就像你在 Aldi 遇到的那种人。他了解所有的零件，然后把它从第 961 名的 Toyota 零件经销商做到了第一名。

turns.en: And he's killing it. He really is good.
turns.zh: 而且他干得风生水起。他是真的很厉害。

turns.en: He started managing a couple different dealerships for the owner. And then he sits down at a Denny's, and the owner is like, hey, you know, I know the plan was for you to run things, but it turns out that my sons need to run it.
turns.zh: 他开始替老板管理好几家不同的经销店。然后他在一家 Denny's 坐下来，老板说，嘿，你知道，我知道原计划是让你来经营，但结果是，我的儿子们需要来经营。

turns.en: Sorry.
turns.zh: 抱歉。

turns.en: And.
turns.zh: 然后……

turns.en: he like, you know, on his heels, he eventually finds somebody else to buy one dealership and that becomes two dealerships and eventually 40 something dealerships and he buys the Utah Jazz. And so that is like, you know, the good story. He developed some skill.
turns.zh: 他就，你知道，猝不及防，最后找到别人买下一家经销店，那变成了两家，最终变成四十来家经销店，然后他买下了 Utah Jazz（爵士队）。所以这就是那个好故事。他培养了某种技能。

turns.en: He really was- Wait, actually on that last point, can you clarify? Okay, so he really gets to know the parts better than anyone else. Can you actually just operationalize that a little bit more? What he contributed to the market, so to speak, such that either at his first place of employment or at his own entrepreneurship, he goes, they go from 961 to one or whatever it is.
turns.zh: 他真的是——等等，最后那一点你能澄清一下吗？好，所以他是真的比谁都更懂零件。你能不能再把这个说得更具体一点？他到底给市场贡献了什么，以至于在第一份工作或者他自己创业时，他从 961 名做到了第 1 名之类的。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.en: So I think it's, you know, when you're dealing with customers being really responsive, understanding what they need and just You know, being hardworking and diligent and delivering and having a reputation for, okay, if I have some need, I'm going to go to this guy.
turns.zh: 所以我觉得，你知道，跟客户打交道时响应特别快，理解他们需要什么，就是勤奋、尽心、能交付，还有个口碑：好，我有什么需求，我就去找这个人。

turns.en: And it grew over time.
turns.zh: 而且它是随时间慢慢做大的。

turns.en: That's one, you know, broader lesson of the book is that it takes a long time, you know, in contrast to the Silicon Valley, move fast and break things. It's often move slow and make things. It takes decades often. So that's kind of, in my view, Larry Miller's the good case.
turns.zh: 这是书里更宽泛的一个教训，就是这需要很长时间。跟 Silicon Valley 那套‘快速行动、打破常规’（move fast and break things）相反，往往是‘慢慢来、把事情做出来’（move slow and make things）。这常常要花几十年。所以在我看来，Larry Miller 是那个好的案例。

turns.en: But the more.
turns.zh: 但那个更……

turns.en: Troublesome case where you have more regulatory capture are other auto dealers who are quite protected. And we can go into the history of auto dealers if you want, but the short version is they have a bunch of legal protections that were meant to protect the little guy from big manufacturers of auto companies. Ford or GM might put a bunch of cars on your lot, and that was hurting the small guy.
turns.zh: 麻烦的案例，是那种有更多监管俘获（regulatory capture）的，也就是另外一些受到相当保护的汽车经销商。如果你想，我们可以讲讲汽车经销商的历史，但简短版本是，他们有一大堆法律保护，本来是为了保护小人物免受大汽车制造商——Ford 或 GM——的欺负。Ford 或 GM 可能会把一大堆车塞到你的场地上，那在伤害小人物。

turns.en: So over.
turns.zh: 所以经过……

turns.en: series of decades, there are a bunch of franchise protections. And then if you go forward to say 2008, when we had the financial crisis, the auto team had to deal with the situation where Chrysler, for example, had three times as many dealerships as Toyota, even though they sold the same number of cars.
turns.zh: 几十年，就有了这一大堆特许经营保护（franchise protections）。然后如果你往后看，比如说到 2008 年金融危机时，汽车团队就得处理这样一个情况：Chrysler 的经销店数量是 Toyota 的三倍，尽管他们卖的车一样多。

turns.en: And so they had all these extra dealers. And why do they have them?
turns.zh: 所以他们有这么多多出来的经销商。他们为什么会有？

turns.en: It's because they have a bunch of protections where you have to pay them off. You have to pay three years of rent and a bunch of things that really don't make sense. And so there's a lot of protections from local competition. There are pretty sweet deals that were in the name of protecting the little guy that don't make a lot of economic sense. So I think some of it is rents. And both of those things are true. And that's partly why things are complex, is that you can have stories like Larry Miller, and you can have regional auto dealers that are getting more money than they probably would because they're getting paid a lot for warranties, for example. that are a little more than what the market would pay them otherwise.
turns.zh: 就是因为他们有一大堆保护，你得把他们打发走——你得付三年的租金还有一堆其实不太合理的东西。所以有很多针对本地竞争的保护。这些是相当划算的买卖，是打着保护小人物的名义搞的，但在经济上不太说得通。所以我觉得其中一部分是租金（rents）。这两件事都是真的，这也正是为什么情况很复杂——你可以有 Larry Miller 这样的故事，也可以有一些区域性汽车经销商，他们拿到的钱可能比应得的多，因为比如他们从保修（warranties）里赚了很多，比市场本来会给他们的要多一些。

turns.en: They have a local monopoly. You can't sell the Toyota within a geographic boundary of the existing dealership. The manufacturer has very limited power to affect that competition in any way to introduce. There's really barriers to entry. That's a big part of it. Then they sell these ancillary services in the dealership where the markups are much higher than on just the immediate sale of the car. The warranty repair the financing is a big source of profits, I think for the dealers. And it's like, well, you know, are you going to buy the, you can get the loan at the dealer. You're going to go to a bank separately when you're buying the car there on the lot. So this like first mover advantage to sell all these ancillary services. And it's a huge part of like the margins and the profitability of these dealerships. And as the economy grows, you still have this like fixed entrant, you know, and like, you can't get a car through any other pipe other than through that pipe. And so they just grab a chunk. as it's passing through.
turns.zh: 他们有本地垄断。你不能在现有经销店的地理边界内卖 Toyota。制造商影响那种竞争、引入新玩家的权力非常有限。真的有进入壁垒（barriers to entry）。这是很大一部分原因。然后他们在经销店里卖这些附加服务（ancillary services），加价比单纯卖车本身要高得多。保修、维修、融资，我想是经销商的一大利润来源。就是说，你知道，你要不要在经销商那儿贷款？你在那块场地上买车时，是就地贷款，还是另外去银行。所以就有这种先发优势来卖所有这些附加服务。这是这些经销店利润率和盈利能力的一大块。而且随着经济增长，你还是有这么个固定的入口，你知道，你没法通过除那根管道以外的任何管道弄到一辆车。所以他们就从中抽走一块，就在它流过去的时候。

turns.en: Yeah, this was really interesting to me in the book because we're used to thinking about antitrust or competition issues as these like big national scale companies, but actually you talk a lot about sort of regionalized competition problems, which was very interesting. I have a bunch of other questions, but I want to ask you one more just on sort of local regulatory protections and loopholes. Can you talk about beer distribution? Because that was a really interesting thing, one to me.
turns.zh: 对，这在书里让我觉得特别有意思，因为我们习惯了把反垄断（antitrust）或竞争问题想成那些大型全国性公司，但其实你们讲了很多那种区域化的竞争问题，这特别有意思。我还有一堆别的问题，但我想再问一个，关于本地的监管保护和漏洞。你能讲讲啤酒分销（beer distribution）吗？因为那是件让我觉得特别有意思的事。

turns.en: We're very amused by the beer distributor. So one of the things for folks that are listening, if you're like walking, like I walked from my home to the office and passed by a truck that says Budweiser on the side. You know, Budweiser doesn't own that truck. A distributor does. You look on the door and there's the name of the distributor. You might see Reyes or somebody like that. These are incredibly wealthy businesses that sit between manufacturers and end users, like bars, restaurants, groceries, and so on. And depending on the state, similar to the auto dealers or these franchise protections, So you have to pass through the distributors and these way these contracts get protected. So then, you know, as demand for beer grows, the distributors just sort of like in the middle, this middle tier was again, sort of protecting, you know, the little guy from the macro brewers. But over time, these little guys have become really big guys.
turns.zh: 我们对啤酒分销商觉得很好笑。所以有一件事，给正在听的朋友，如果你像我从家走到办公室的路上，经过一辆侧面写着 Budweiser 的卡车——你知道，Budweiser 并不拥有那辆卡车，是分销商拥有的。你看车门上，会有分销商的名字，你可能会看到 Reyes 之类的。这些是极其有钱的企业，它们夹在制造商和终端用户——比如酒吧、餐厅、杂货店等等——之间。而且视州而定，跟汽车经销商或者那些特许经营保护类似，所以你必须经过分销商，这些合同就这样受到保护。所以随着啤酒需求增长，分销商就夹在中间……这个中间层（middle tier）本来是保护小人物免受大酿酒商欺负的。但随着时间推移，这些小人物变成了真正的大人物。

turns.en: Um, and you know, the idea was you didn't want the big brewers to dominate distribution as well as the actual selling of the product.
turns.zh: 嗯，你知道，那个想法是你不希望大酿酒商既主导分销、又主导产品的实际销售。

turns.en: That's right. And it's sort of emerged post prohibition as this like sort of system let's avoid the system, the situation where, um, the manufacturers have so much power over the rest of the system in terms of what is available. But then the distributors end up having just a ton of power and they get super rich. So they show up within the jet data a lot. And there was this like conference in San Antonio. And the mayor called the lobbyists who organized the conference, was like, you know, this is amazing. I've never seen so many jets at the San Antonio airport as when the beer wholesalers were there.
turns.zh: 没错。这算是禁酒令（prohibition）之后出现的一套体系，就是为了避免那种制造商对整个体系——就什么是可获得的——有过大权力的情况。但结果分销商最后拥有了巨大的权力，而且变得超级有钱。所以他们在飞机数据里经常出现。当时在 San Antonio 有个会议，市长把组织那个会议的游说者叫来，说，你知道，这太惊人了，我在 San Antonio 机场从没见过这么多飞机，就像啤酒批发商在那儿的时候那样。

turns.en: You mentioned a disagreement or a different interpretation than capital picketing and size, et cetera. What is the essence of the conclusions or the things that you've discovered today? that you feel like someone coming at the wealth inequality question from their work, you would have a different interpretation of it. But we've never actually had either one of them on the show, so maybe we'll get them on soon because we should. But what is the sort of the crux of how you see things differently?
turns.zh: 你提到过跟《Capital》、Piketty 和规模等等有不同的解读或分歧。你们今天发现的这些结论、这些东西，其核心是什么？就是那种，你觉得一个从他们的工作出发来看财富不平等问题的人，会对此有不同的解读。不过我们其实从没请过他们任何一位上节目，所以也许我们很快会请他们，因为我们该请。但你们看事情的角度，其关键的分歧在哪儿？

turns.en: So we joke that our book is kind of like pickety with people. So if you happen to read Capital, which is a difficult read, I think we actually also joke that our book we wrote so people could read it, not just collect it.
turns.zh: 所以我们开玩笑说，我们这本书有点像‘有人的 Piketty’（Piketty with people）。所以如果你碰巧读过《Capital》，那是本难读的书——我想我们还开玩笑说，我们写这本书是为了让人能读，而不只是拿来收藏。

turns.en: Because that book, it's a really good read.
turns.zh: 因为那本书，真的很好读。

turns.en: I'm just going to reiterate that.
turns.zh: 我就再强调一遍这点。

turns.en: So it's like, we're going to have, you know, that book is like the top 1% is this kind of nameless faceless entity. Um, and they're just generating capital income. And so you kind of are meant to think about almost gilded age monopolists who have massive companies and are just collecting the rents or the capital income or the interest or whatever. And, um, it's about this accumulation of massive troves of wealth that are generating this almost passive return. And we're saying, well, actually, when you look at the data, it's actually more this like these millions of private business owners who are actively owning and operating businesses in a large case. Their concentrated portfolio is really the business is kind of the main asset. And it's not really just financial capital. It's kind of like human capital is a pretty important part of it. Broadly defined, it's sort of like the networks, the experience. Maybe it's like having access to the contract or the special like market position, that's an important asset. But that's like sort of a different story about who's really rich. That's sort of this more active kind of human. And yeah, there's good, bad and ugly of the humans there. But that's kind of the distinction I think that we draw.
turns.zh: 所以，你知道，《Capital》那本书里，最富的 1% 是某种没有名字、没有面孔的实体。他们就是在产生资本收入。所以你多少会被引导去想，几乎像是镀金时代（gilded age）的垄断者，拥有庞大的公司，就是收着租金、或者资本收入、或者利息什么的。它讲的是这种巨额财富宝库的积累，产生着这种几乎被动的回报。而我们要说的是，实际上，当你看数据时，更多的是这几百万私有企业主，他们在主动地拥有和经营着企业，在很多情况下，他们高度集中的资产组合其实就是那家企业，企业算是主要资产。而且它并不真的只是金融资本（financial capital）。人力资本（human capital）也是相当重要的一部分。广义地讲，它更像是人脉网络、经验。也许是能拿到那份合同，或者某种特殊的市场地位，那是种重要的资产。但这就是一个关于‘谁才是真正有钱人’的不同故事。它更像是主动的、有人的那种。是的，那里的人有好、有坏、也有丑。但这大概就是我们所做的那个区分。

turns.en: Since you talk to a lot of these people, I have a sort of anthropological question, but do they see themselves as wealthy? Because we touched on this in the beginning, but everything is sort of like shaded as small business ownership, entrepreneurs. You talk to a lot of people who like Did start from humble beginnings, but now have millions and millions of dollars. Do they do they see themselves as the rich, as the one percent?
turns.zh: 既然你们跟这些人聊了很多，我有个有点人类学（anthropological）的问题：他们把自己看成有钱人吗？因为我们开头就碰到了这点，但一切都被蒙上了‘小企业主’‘创业者’的色彩。你们跟很多人聊过，他们确实是从卑微的起点开始的，但如今有几百万几千万美元。他们把自己看成富人、看成那 1% 吗？

turns.en: Usually they they have a pretty good idea. Often it's because it takes so long to get wealthy there. You know, they've gone through the life cycle. So one of my favorite characters that we talk to in the book is Dick Portillo.
turns.zh: 通常他们心里挺有数的。往往是因为，变富要花太长时间，他们走完了整个人生周期。所以我们在书里聊到的、我最喜欢的一个人物之一，是 Dick Portillo。

turns.en: And he started he grew up in the projects.
turns.zh: 他是在……他是在公共住宅区（projects）里长大的。

turns.en: Of Chicago, the Cabrini greens, and he didn't know how to make a hot dog and then started a hot dog company and was washing the dishes.
turns.zh: 在 Chicago 的 Cabrini-Green，他当时不知道怎么做热狗，然后开了一家热狗公司，还自己洗碗。

turns.en: By hand because there wasn't running water.
turns.zh: 用手洗，因为没有自来水。

turns.en: And he ended up over decades selling a lot of hot dogs to become a billionaire. And I think it's a really useful example because it shows like, well, do you have to have market power to be a billionaire? No, you can actually sell hot dogs to super competitive industry.
turns.zh: 然后他花了数十年，卖了大量热狗，成了亿万富翁。我觉得这是个非常有用的例子，因为它表明，你要成为亿万富翁，非得有市场势力（market power）吗？不，你其实可以卖热狗，在一个超级竞争的行业里。

turns.en: And then is he rich? Well, he has a really big penthouse.
turns.zh: 那他有钱吗？嗯，他有一套很大的顶层公寓（penthouse）。

turns.en: He's got a yacht called Top Dog, which is just a great name for the yacht. And so it depends on when you're talking to him. I think when you find him in his 30s washing stuff by hand, he does not feel rich. But when he's got a yacht and a huge IPO that they couldn't send him a check because he's his bank account wasn't sophisticated enough to take the check when he was just like, I'm getting on my yacht and leaving. I think he knew. The short answer is it depends on when in their lifetimes, because it does really take a long time. There's another woman who talked to, she spent two decades making frozen quiche. Oh yeah, the quiche lady. Yeah. And it was pretty tenuous for a long time before she got some big contracts to go through. And so I don't think she felt... that wealthy from her business. It seemed like it was losing money until it really wasn't.
turns.zh: 他有一艘叫 Top Dog 的游艇，这名字对游艇来说真是太棒了。所以这取决于你什么时候跟他聊。我想你在他三十几岁、还在那儿手洗东西的时候找到他，他不觉得自己有钱。但当他有了一艘游艇、又做了一大笔 IPO，以至于银行都没法给他开张支票，因为他的银行账户还不够高级、接不下那张支票，而他当时就说‘我要上我的游艇走了’——我想他心里有数。简短的答案是，这取决于他们在人生中的哪个阶段，因为变富确实要花很长时间。还有另一位我们聊过的女士，她花了二十年做冷冻乳蛋饼（frozen quiche）。哦对，那位‘乳蛋饼女士’（quiche lady）。对。而且在她拿到一些大合同之前，很长时间都相当岌岌可危。所以我不觉得她觉得自己因为这门生意有多富。看起来它一直在亏钱，直到它真的不亏了。

turns.en: This is maybe more of a sociological question than an economics question, but I think it relates to who feels rich and who doesn't. When I think about coastal rich, and by that I mean San Francisco or New York City rich, I often think about heads of really gigantic... heavily bureaucratic, layered hierarchical organizations. I imagine someone like Jamie Dimon or the CEO, there are numerous layers. A, they're often very educated, and there are also going to be just numerous layers of the organization, and there will be people who work at J.P. Morgan or whatever who never interact ever with the CEO, etc., Whereas in my mind, the sort of everyday millionaires, the head of the beverage distributor and the car dealership, in my mind, I suspect these organizations are like that CEO is probably much more in touch on some level on a day-to-day basis with the mass of like the workers at that organization, maybe on the floor with them, many cases like at a dealership, etc., And I'm curious if that resonates and whether that's sort of like, you know, when we think about sort of, you know, someone who has a yacht is obviously mega rich, but on the, that's unquestionable, but also that just on a day-to-day basis, I suspect they have a lot more connection and like interaction with capital W workers than many is sort of like the coastal rich do.
turns.zh: 这也许更是个社会学问题，而不是经济学问题，但我觉得它关系到谁觉得自己有钱、谁不觉得。当我想到‘沿海的富’——我指的是 San Francisco 或者 New York City 那种富——我常常想到的是那些极其庞大的、官僚层层叠叠的等级制组织的头头。我会想象像 Jamie Dimon 那样的人，或者那种 CEO，有很多层级。第一，他们往往受教育程度很高；而且组织里也会有很多层级，会有一些在 J.P. Morgan 之类工作的人，永远、永远都不会跟 CEO 打交道，等等。而在我的脑子里，那种日常的百万富翁——饮料分销商的头头、汽车经销商的头头——在我看来，我猜想这些组织的 CEO 在某种程度上，日常跟那一大堆‘工人’接触得多得多，也许就在现场跟他们一起，很多情况下比如在经销店等等。我很好奇这是否说得通，以及这是否是那种……你知道，当我们想到某个有游艇的人，显然是超级有钱，那是毋庸置疑的；但同时，就在日常层面，我猜想他们跟大写 W 的‘工人’（capital W workers）有很多的连接和互动，比很多那种‘沿海的富’要多。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.en: So like the Portillo, when he was growing the business, They didn't have offices for the managers because he wanted the people to be on the floor all the time. There was a bit of a marine ethic that he brought to running this business. He was there for opening. He was very detail-oriented.
turns.zh: 所以像 Portillo，当他在把企业做大的时候，他们不给经理们设办公室，因为他想让人们一直在现场。他把一种海军陆战队的作风（marine ethic）带到了经营这家企业上。开门的时候他在。他非常注重细节。

turns.en: He had no investors.
turns.zh: 他没有投资人。

turns.en: He owned all the real estate. He tried to take no debt, reinvesting every dollar. He had kids, but it was pretty clear when he was moving into his 80s, this is not a family business. This is Dick's business. And there's kind of a relentlessness to that character that I think we see in many of the stories. The first generation founders look like that.
turns.zh: 他拥有所有的房地产。他尽量不负债，把每一美元都再投资回去。他有孩子，但很清楚，当他进入八十几岁时，这不是一门家族生意，这是 Dick 的生意。这个角色身上有种不懈的劲头，我想我们在很多故事里都能看到。第一代创始人就是那样的。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.en: One thing that stood out to me is all of these people don't seem to have hobbies.
turns.zh: 有一点让我印象深刻，就是这些人好像都没有爱好。

turns.en: They hate hobbies. Yeah.
turns.zh: 他们讨厌爱好。对。

turns.en: They hate hobbies.
turns.zh: 他们讨厌爱好。

turns.en: John Osher is so funny.
turns.zh: John Osher 特别有意思。

turns.en: Dr.
turns.zh: 博士……

turns.en: John, he's not a doctor, who started the $ 5 electric toothbrush and sold that business after having sold other businesses before and probably had enough money before starting that business. But he tried to take up golf from Florida. He's like, So bored by it. Maybe not a great swing.
turns.zh: John，他不是博士，他做起了那种 5 美元的电动牙刷，把这门生意卖了——在此之前他也卖过别的生意，在做那门生意之前大概就已经很有钱了。但他试着打高尔夫——他在 Florida——他说，太无聊了。也许球技不怎么样。

turns.en: I don't know.
turns.zh: 我不知道。

turns.en: But went back and started this $ 5 toothbrush business in the dot-com era, which is exactly the kind of company you would think would make you hundreds of millions of dollars during the dot-com era. It's only $ 5 electric toothbrushes. But that's what he did because he just couldn't sit still. I mean, he had a personality, clearly, because even as a kid, his first business was was um don't tell your son the story his first business so his parents just took like one of those painting classes where you like have models come in and do the like the nude paintings and they hid the paintings from like five seven year old i don't know like uh in the attic and he would charge a nickel to his friends.
turns.zh: 但他又回去做起了这门 5 美元牙刷的生意，就在互联网泡沫（dot-com）时代，而那恰恰是那种你会以为能在 dot-com 时代让你赚几亿美元的公司。它只是 5 美元的电动牙刷。但那就是他做的，因为他就是坐不住。我是说，他显然有那样的个性，因为即便小时候，他的第一门生意是——别跟你儿子讲这个故事——他的第一门生意，是他父母上了那种绘画课，就是有模特来、画那种裸体画的课，他们把画藏在阁楼里，不让像五六岁、七岁的他看到，我不知道，然后他就向朋友们收五美分（a nickel）。

turns.en: To look at the paintings i would love this.
turns.zh: 来看那些画。我太喜欢这个了。

turns.en: Yes that's the best margins of any business he ever started.
turns.zh: 是的，那是他做过的所有生意里利润最高的。

turns.en: He can't uh He can't listen to this episode.
turns.zh: 他不能……他不能听这一期。

turns.en: I'll stick to the children's book.
turns.zh: 我还是就写那本儿童书吧。

turns.en: Yeah, yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊，是啊。

turns.en: Maybe you just.
turns.zh: 也许你就……

turns.en: Paint still lifes.
turns.zh: 画静物（still lifes）。

turns.en: Can we talk a little bit about, you mentioned dentists, and I'm sort of curious whether dentists or doctors, what is their role in the story of the medical profession and how rich can they get?
turns.zh: 我们能聊聊……你提到了牙医，我很好奇牙医或者医生，他们在医疗行业的故事里扮演什么角色，他们能有多有钱？

turns.en: Yeah, no, that's a great question because there's kind of the Dick Portillo's more tactile, blue-collar rich, and then there are the more white-collar ones. But if you own eight dental practices— you can be really rich. I mean, I think if you're just a normal dentist, you have a pretty good life. But if you own a few offices, you can have a great life. Dentists have some amazing stats. I think they're number 21 on our list of top pass-through four-digit industries by profit. And if you add up all the revenue of dentists in America, it exceeds the revenue generated by the NFL, the NBA, MLB, basically all professional sports, and dentists are earning more. The joke we like to tell is that everybody's got teeth. And so if you own several of these, this is great. And then they also are in every congressional district. And so when you think about things like, oh, let's include dental services and Medicare, for example, they lobby against that to be like, well, we don't want price pressure from the government. We want to make sure So there is a bit of regulatory might, and that's really the case more for doctors, too.
turns.zh: 对，不，这是个好问题，因为有那种 Dick Portillo 式的、更动手、蓝领的富，然后也有更白领的那种。但如果你拥有八家牙科诊所，你可以非常有钱。我是说，我觉得如果你只是个普通牙医，你日子过得挺好的。但如果你拥有几家诊所，你能过得非常棒。牙医有一些惊人的数据。我想他们在我们那份按利润排名的顶级穿透式四位数行业榜单上排第 21。如果你把全美所有牙医的收入加起来，它超过了 NFL、NBA、MLB 产生的收入——基本上是所有职业体育——而牙医赚得更多。我们爱讲的那个笑话是，每个人都有牙齿。所以如果你拥有好几家这样的诊所，那就太棒了。而且他们遍布每一个国会选区。所以当你想到，哦，比如把牙科服务纳入 Medicare（联邦医疗保险），他们会游说反对，说，我们不想来自政府的价格压力。我们要确保……所以确实有一点监管势力（regulatory might），而这对医生来说更是如此。

turns.en: Yeah, the doctors showed up in one of our early statistical breakdowns. We were trying to figure out, okay, who are these people entering all this pass-through income? We said, what are the top four-digit industries and the top 1%? Doctors' offices was number one. So this is like their industry codes by the BEA. And so four-digit, there are about 300 industries in the four-digit system. So that's like a pretty... We're fine. Like doctor's office is different from dentist's office is different from like a physical therapy type industry. As an example, within services, doctors were number one in terms of the number of amount of profits. And they had just a ton of them.
turns.zh: 对，医生出现在我们早期的一份统计拆分里。我们当时想搞清楚，好，这些申报所有这些穿透式收入的人是谁？我们说，在最富的 1% 里，前几名的四位数行业是什么？医生诊所（doctors' offices）排第一。所以这是 BEA（经济分析局）按行业代码分的。所以四位数，那个四位数体系里大约有 300 个行业。所以那算是相当……我们没问题。就是说医生诊所跟牙医诊所不一样，也跟那种理疗（physical therapy）行业不一样。举个例子，在服务业里，就利润的数额而言，医生排第一。而且他们的数量多得惊人。

turns.en: Is it true that like dentists, like they're all really bored. So they get really like tempted to finance films. Isn't that like a big thing where it's like filmmakers, like go to dentists, like this would be more exciting than teeth put a hundred thousand dollars into this film.
turns.zh: 是不是真的，牙医们都特别无聊，所以他们特别容易被诱惑去投资电影？这是不是个大现象，就是电影制作人去找牙医，说，这比补牙刺激多了，往这部电影里投十万美元吧。

turns.en: They are, I think, sitting on pools of cash and maybe they don't have so many ideas of what to do with it. And so they make for maybe easy targets. And because it's a big pool of cash, you know, there's a lot of fishing to be done in that pool.
turns.zh: 他们，我觉得，坐在一池池现金上，也许没那么多点子怎么用。所以他们也许是容易下手的目标。而且因为那是一大池现金，你知道，在那池子里有很多‘鱼’可钓。

turns.en: So speaking of dentists and doctors, this reminds me, you have a working example in the book showing how the S-Corp pass-through tax benefits actually works for, I think it was for an anesthesiologist. And the one who is in private practice who has their own S-Corp pays less tax than the one who's employed and earning income. What exactly are we incentivizing or supposed to be incentivizing through the tax code here? Because again, these are two people who are ostensibly doing the same jobs. One is paying a lot less tax than the other one by virtue of the pass-through arrangement.
turns.zh: 说到牙医和医生，这让我想起来，你们书里有个现成的例子，展示 S 型公司（S-Corp）的穿透式税收优惠实际上是怎么起作用的，我记得是拿一位麻醉科医生（anesthesiologist）举例。那个自己开私人诊所、拥有自己 S 型公司的人，比那个受雇、赚工资收入的人缴更少的税。我们到底在这里通过税法激励、或者说本该激励的是什么？因为再说一次，这是两个表面上做着同样工作的人，一个仅仅因为穿透式的安排就比另一个缴少得多的税。

turns.en: Yeah, so we are taxing salaries at a different rate than taxing business income. And so that anesthesiologist that runs most of the business through the S Corp, is not paying payroll tax, not paying like ACA sort of surcharge, which is uncapped Medicare tax on the profits that come through, which is maybe particularly galling because they're billing Medicare for so much services and they themselves on their mostly labor income aren't paying the Medicare tax on it. So, you know, there is a minimum level of compensation, which the IRS rules say you're supposed to pay yourself in wages. So you pay payroll tax on that. everything above that reasonable compensation limit is kind of profit and just falls in this other bucket. And then in the 2017 reform, they brought down the pass-through rate even further from, say, the top rate of 37% to below 30%. They put in these guardrails for doctors and skilled service professions so they couldn't get that rate. But there are strategies that certain ones take to try and move a bunch of the ancillary services again, or the surgery piece, or the Maybe they rent some real estate back. And so they can shift more and more of that income, I think, into forms that then get that below 30% rate. Whereas the surgeon that's working in the hospital system as a salaried worker is paying the top individual tax rate, 37%. The payroll tax, another 3%. You have all the state and local taxes. The cap on state and local tax deductions applies to that salaried worker. But if you run all your income through the business, then the states have allowed them to basically take the deductions through the business instead and get that uncapped.
turns.zh: 对，所以我们对工资征的税率跟对营业收入征的不一样。所以那位麻醉科医生，大部分业务通过 S 型公司走，就不缴工资税（payroll tax），不缴那种 ACA（平价医疗法案）附加费——就是对流进来的利润征的、不封顶的 Medicare 税——这可能尤其让人恼火，因为他们向 Medicare 开了那么多服务的账单，而他们自己，在其大部分是劳动收入上，却不为此缴 Medicare 税。所以，你知道，有个最低报酬水平，IRS 的规则说你该给自己发这么多工资，你就为那部分缴工资税。超过那个‘合理报酬’（reasonable compensation）上限的一切，都算利润，就落进另一个筐里。然后在 2017 年的改革里，他们把穿透式税率进一步降了下来，从比如 37% 的最高税率降到 30% 以下。他们给医生和技术型服务行业设了这些护栏（guardrails），让他们拿不到那个税率。但有一些策略，某些人会用来把更多的那些附加服务、或者手术那块，也许还有把一些房地产回租（rent back），转移出去。所以他们能把越来越多的那种收入，我想，转移进那些能拿到 30% 以下税率的形式里。而在医院体系里当受薪员工的那位外科医生，缴的是最高的个人税率 37%，工资税再加 3%，还有所有的州和地方税。州和地方税抵扣（SALT deduction）的上限适用于那个受薪员工。但如果你把所有收入都通过企业走，那么各州已经允许他们基本上通过企业来拿这些抵扣，从而不受那个上限约束。

turns.en: What's the thinking behind this? We just want lots of small businesses to be created. And so here are some tax benefits.
turns.zh: 这背后的思路是什么？我们就是想要大量的小企业被创建出来，所以给一些税收优惠。

turns.en: I think it's kind of an unintended consequence of trying to simplify the tax code for the mom and pops in the small business.
turns.zh: 我觉得这是想为夫妻店（mom and pops）、为小企业简化税法的一个意外后果（unintended consequence）。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.en: And then people sort of look at the rules and say, well, how do I minimize my tax given the rules are what they are? And then how do we protect those loopholes that sort of pop up over time? I like to think of the tax code like a house that sort of depreciates over time and you kind of need to like invest in it, like repair windows, replace the floor, this kind of thing. These loopholes are like the depreciation that's applied to this house over time. The reason they've been so persistent, we haven't fixed them, is because it turns out that like a quarter of federal elected officials are also pass-through business owners.
turns.zh: 然后人们就去看这些规则，说，好，在规则就是这么定的情况下，我怎么把我的税降到最低？然后我们又怎么去保护那些随时间冒出来的漏洞？我喜欢把税法想成一栋会随时间折旧（depreciate）的房子，你得往里投资，比如修窗户、换地板，这类事。这些漏洞就像是随时间对这栋房子计提的折旧。它们之所以这么顽固、我们一直没修好，是因为结果发现，大约四分之一的联邦民选官员本身也是穿透式企业主。

turns.en: Yeah, this is always like my impression is like, you know, pick a state, Iowa or Ohio. And it's like, you know, I get some politician who's worth a hundred million dollars, but I, and they often tend to do very well. And they like position themselves as like, you know, popular among the working class voters and, And they probably do connect well with them in part because they like, this is what I was going back to. They're on the shop floor. They probably do connect with those voters better than like, you know, CEO of a big bank who's like completely disconnected from them. But on the tax question specifically, you know, when it comes to the prospect of raising revenue for the government or raising taxes, you get a litany of issues. So, A, no one likes paying higher taxes, period. Then there's you get to say, well, you know, we don't want to disincentivize entrepreneurship or success or whatever. And taxes are bad for that reason. And then there's the third layer. It's like, well, even if we want, even if we want to have higher taxes and even if we weren't worried about that, it would be impossible. And the rich always find a way. And so it'd be self-defeating. There's no way to like, actually, you can't do it. They'll find some loophole or whatever. And that third part I'm really curious about, is that real? Or in your research, if there were the political will to raise taxes, are there straightforward ways to do it?
turns.zh: 对，这一直是我的印象，就是，你挑一个州，Iowa 或者 Ohio，然后，你知道，我遇到某个身价一亿美元的政客，但他们往往做得非常好。他们喜欢把自己定位成，你知道，在工薪阶层选民里很受欢迎。而且他们可能确实跟这些人连接得很好，部分是因为——这就是我前面要说的——他们就在车间现场（shop floor）。他们跟那些选民的连接，可能确实比某个大银行的 CEO 好，那位 CEO 跟他们完全脱节。但具体到税收问题上，你知道，一谈到为政府增加收入或者加税的前景，你就会听到一连串的说辞。第一，没人喜欢缴更高的税，就这样。然后你就可以说，我们不想打击创业或者成功之类的积极性，所以出于那个原因税是坏的。然后还有第三层，就是，即便我们想、即便我们想要更高的税、即便我们不担心那个，那也不可能。富人总有办法。所以那会适得其反。根本没办法真的做到，你办不到。他们会找到某个漏洞什么的。而这第三部分我特别好奇，那是真的吗？还是在你们的研究里，如果真有加税的政治意愿，是有直截了当的办法做到的？

turns.en: Yeah, so it's certainly real. I mean, we could start with the most recent. So first of all, you asked about Iowa and Ohio. So Ohio, one of the senators is Bernie Moreno, who's an auto dealer. So that's a great one. And he had a proposal with Elizabeth Warren to shore up Social Security.
turns.zh: 对，所以它确实是真的。我是说，我们可以从最近的说起。首先，你问到了 Iowa 和 Ohio。Ohio 的其中一位参议员是 Bernie Moreno，他是个汽车经销商。所以那是个很好的例子。他跟 Elizabeth Warren 一起提了个提案，要巩固社会保障（Social Security）。

turns.en: How do you want to do it?
turns.zh: 他们想怎么做？

turns.en: You put it on the payroll of all these salaried workers. There's no mention of these very wealthy business owners, like it's all salaries. So the anesthesiologist that you were talking about before, one of them is getting off, you know, scot-free and the other one is paying a lot more. So I think That's one very recent example.
turns.zh: 你把它加到所有这些受薪员工的工资上。完全没提这些非常有钱的企业主，就像全是工资似的。所以你之前说的那位麻醉科医生，其中一个基本逍遥自在、毫发无损，而另一个缴得多得多。所以我觉得那是一个非常近期的例子。

turns.en: Now, it's interesting.
turns.zh: 现在，这挺有意思的。

turns.en: We've been talking to folks on the Hill about, you know, what the prospect of raising taxes on the rich is. One natural place to start is this trillion dollar tax cut that was part of the One Big Beautiful Business. bill that no one likes to talk about. And even among Democratic staffers, there's a lot of reticence of like, oh, I don't know, small business. And you're like, this is not small. You know, if you take all pass-through income, only 20% of it is actually small business, according to an old Treasury study. The vast majority are big businesses that happen to be private. And so I think the most realistic thing, if you can't get rid of some of these loopholes, is to limit them by income.
turns.zh: 我们一直在跟国会山（the Hill）上的人聊，你知道，对富人加税的前景如何。一个自然的起点，是那项一万亿美元的减税，它是 One Big Beautiful Bill 的一部分，没人喜欢谈它。而且即便在民主党的幕僚里，也有很多不情愿，就是，哦，我不知道，小企业嘛。你就会说，这不小。你知道，如果你把所有穿透式收入算进去，根据财政部一份旧研究，只有 20% 才是真正的小企业。绝大多数是碰巧私有的大企业。所以我觉得最现实的，如果你没法废除其中一些漏洞的话，就是按收入来限制它们。

turns.en: And that, to me, seems like one path.
turns.zh: 而那，对我来说，似乎是一条路。

turns.en: When you say limit them by income, explain that further.
turns.zh: 你说按收入来限制，把这个再解释一下。

turns.en: So, you know, say you cannot get a deduction that takes your rate from 37 to 30 if you have income in excess of. a million dollars or 400K. You pick the number that, I don't like these numbers, but that would be one mechanism for saying, okay, somebody has more than a million dollars in business income. They are doing very well. You can't plausibly call them small.
turns.zh: 所以，你知道，比如说，如果你的收入超过一百万美元或者 40 万美元——你挑个数，我不喜欢这些数字——你就不能拿到那个把你税率从 37 降到 30 的抵扣。那就是一种机制，用来表达：好，某人的营业收入超过一百万美元，他们做得非常好，你没法可信地称他们为‘小’企业。

turns.en: This reminds me, actually, can we talk about the role of private equity in wealth creation? Because again, when we talk about a lot of these businesses, whether it's HVAC or, I don't know, veterinarian services or dentist offices, A lot of the exits come in the form of a PE buyout.
turns.zh: 这其实让我想起来，我们能聊聊私募股权（private equity）在财富创造里的角色吗？因为再说一次，当我们谈到这些企业里的很多——不管是 HVAC、我不知道、兽医服务还是牙科诊所——很多退出（exits）是以 PE 收购（buyout）的形式发生的。

turns.en: We love this line from your colleague, Matt Levine, who tells this joke, what am I doing after business school? Oh, I'm going to work for a prestigious private equity firm in San Francisco so I can run their plumbing company in Mississippi. And I teach private equity to MBA students and I talk about these unglamorous deals. So we're talking about founder-owned firms and more than half of the deal, the typical deals in the pipeline from private equity are going to be founder- generated firms that maybe there's no natural successor. So private equity sort of comes in and said, we can take the baton and maybe we'll be willing to pay a pretty high price because we can see the growth trajectory for it. And so they're looking for these unglamorous businesses that are quite profitable. Maybe they have some competitive advantage because of either a barrier to entry or established brand and customer network and so on. And they're going to go in and take it over for the founder who doesn't really want to give it to the kids or doesn't have a kid that wants to take over the plumbing company So private equity portfolios, if you go below the glamorous New York job where you go like where they're actually on site, what are they looking at? It's a mid-market manufacturer making cabinets or it's sort of the shade store or something like that. These regional businesses that they want to grow further, maybe consolidate a few of them. Maybe they can list it or break it up or whatever down the road. But it's transformed finance in a way because a lot of capital is flowing.
turns.zh: 我们很喜欢你们同事 Matt Levine 的那个段子，他讲这个笑话：商学院毕业后我要干嘛？哦，我要去 San Francisco 一家声名显赫的私募股权公司上班，这样我就能去经营他们在 Mississippi 的水管公司了。我给 MBA 学生讲私募股权，我会讲这些不光鲜的交易。所以我们说的是创始人持有的公司，而且在私募股权典型的项目储备（pipeline）里，超过一半的交易会是创始人创办的公司，也许没有天然的接班人。所以私募股权就进来，说，我们能接棒，也许我们愿意出个相当高的价，因为我们能看到它的增长轨迹。所以他们在找这些不光鲜、但相当赚钱的企业。也许它们因为进入壁垒、或者成熟的品牌和客户网络等等，有某种竞争优势。然后他们就要进去，从创始人手里接过来——那个创始人不太愿意把公司交给孩子，或者没有一个想接手水管公司的孩子。所以私募股权的投资组合，如果你看到那些不光鲜的 New York 岗位之下、他们真正在现场看的东西，那是什么？是家做橱柜的中端市场制造商，或者是那种窗帘店（shade store）之类的。这些区域性企业，他们想进一步做大，也许整合几家，也许日后能让它上市、或者拆分，或者怎样。但它以某种方式改变了金融，因为大量资本正在流动。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.en: And there's the end point.
turns.zh: 而且有那个终点。

turns.en: Are these search funds? Is that what they are called? Like, I've heard that term. And I'm curious. I've been like seeing the, you know, people on Twitter, but they like, oh, all this stuff. I'm rolling up cabinet makers or whatever. pool servicing providers or lawnmowers, or like, I imagine like a pest repellent is a pretty big thing, but I've been reading about them for like a long time now. Is there still more juice for the squeeze? Is there still a bunch of these boomer businesses where the kids don't want it? And in theory, you could take over the local lawn maintenance company and make more money or how much is left there?
turns.zh: 这些是搜索基金（search funds）吗？它们是这么叫的吗？我听说过这个词。我很好奇，我一直在看 Twitter 上的那些人，他们说，哦，我在把橱柜制造商、或者泳池维护服务商、或者割草机、或者……我猜驱虫（pest repellent）是个挺大的东西，但我读这些已经读了很长时间了。这块还有油水可榨吗？还剩一大堆这种‘婴儿潮一代’（boomer）的企业、孩子不想要的吗？理论上你可以接手本地那家草坪养护公司然后赚更多钱，还是说那儿还剩多少？

turns.en: Well, we think about the great wealth transfer, right? This tens of trillions of dollars of wealth in the sort of silent generation or baby boomer generation, more than half of that is like in the form of business wealth, but there's a huge amount of business wealth that's coming. And there aren't necessarily kids or great, you know, people who want to run it from within those businesses. Some of them are too small to attract private equity and trust. And so, yeah, so I see students first, it was like a few students that knew about the search fund thing. I started in 2014 teaching and I was talking about search funds. So this is like a student spends two years, usually have a partner, looking for one of these businesses that's kind of too small to attract private equity interest. So they can do a mini LBO. They can do a mini buyout. If they find a good candidate, the investors that funded the search will do a second step. So there's optionality for the investors that makes it such that even the median return in search funds is negative. Most of them lose a little bit of money because the search doesn't work. But the average return is like low 20s, I think. And the sort of data is a little hard to come by. But I think the people who are trying to do a good job of comprehensively measuring it. And it's rolling up pest control businesses. One of the most successful ones I talk about in class is drug treatment facilities in California. There was like a huge growth in demand for that, unfortunately. And these facilities, running them, running them well, doing the billing. Doing the kind of, you know, they're running those businesses is complicated. A lot of regulatory things you have to manage as well. But that person, that was like 100x investment for the investors and for the founder. Oh, I could go to banking and then maybe flip into PE and then maybe get like junior partner and get up there in like a decade, 15 years or something. Or I could like start this business and run a business, get all this weird experience doing deals, industry learning, raising money, operating something. like kind of bootstrap my way into being a seasoned founder and an executive and own 20% of the company on the other end if it does well.
turns.zh: 嗯，我们会想到那场‘伟大的财富转移’（great wealth transfer），对吧？这几万亿美元的财富在‘沉默一代’（silent generation）或者婴儿潮一代手里，其中超过一半是以企业财富的形式存在的，但有大量的企业财富正在到来。而且不一定有孩子、或者有那种从企业内部想接手的人。其中一些太小了，吸引不了私募股权和信托。所以，是啊，我先看到学生——最早是几个学生知道搜索基金这东西。我从 2014 年开始教书，就在讲搜索基金。所以这是这样一个东西：一个学生花两年时间，通常有个搭档，去找这些企业里的一个，就是那种太小、吸引不了私募股权兴趣的企业。这样他们就能做个迷你 LBO（mini LBO），做个迷你收购。如果他们找到一个好的候选，那些资助这次‘搜索’的投资人会做第二步。所以对投资人来说有种期权性（optionality），这使得即便是搜索基金的中位数回报也是负的。它们大多数会亏一点点钱，因为搜索没成。但平均回报大概在 20% 出头，我想。这类数据有点难拿到。但我觉得那些试图全面衡量它的人做得不错。它是在把驱虫企业整合起来。我在课上讲的最成功的案例之一，是 California 的戒毒治疗机构（drug treatment facilities）。不幸的是，那方面的需求增长巨大。而经营这些机构、经营好它们、做账单……你知道，经营那些企业很复杂，还有很多监管上的事要管。但那个人，对投资人和创始人来说都是 100 倍（100x）的投资回报。哦，我本可以去银行，然后也许跳进 PE，然后也许当上初级合伙人（junior partner），在十年、十五年之类的时间内爬到那个位置。或者我可以创办这门生意、经营一门生意，获得所有这些奇特的经验——做交易、行业学习、募资、经营某样东西——就像 bootstrap 式地把自己打造成一个经验丰富的创始人和高管，如果做得好，另一端还能拥有公司 20% 的股份。

turns.en: This also reminds me, in terms of just creating an environment that encourages entrepreneurs, you actually found some really interesting or did some really interesting research showing that if you are in a place with a lot of entrepreneurs, you are more likely to be a business owner yourself.
turns.zh: 这也让我想起来，就营造一个鼓励创业者的环境而言，你们其实发现了一些、或者做了一些非常有意思的研究，表明如果你身处一个有很多创业者的地方，你自己更可能成为企业主。

turns.en: Yeah. So one of the cool data things, you know, to go back to the very beginning, when we built this data set that for the first time linked owners to businesses and their workers, we could track every single new firm in America since 2000. So we have the best data on entrepreneurs that has ever existed. And we can say, you know, how many people are going to start businesses if they're poor, if they grow up in Salt Lake City versus Mississippi.
turns.zh: 对。所以那些很酷的数据事情之一——你知道，回到最开始，当我们搭建了这个数据集，第一次把所有者跟企业和他们的员工关联起来，我们就能追踪自 2000 年以来美国每一家新公司。所以我们拥有关于创业者的、有史以来最好的数据。我们就能说，你知道，如果一个人穷，或者在 Salt Lake City 长大、对比在 Mississippi 长大，会有多少人去创业。

turns.en: So Salt Lake, the probability you start a star business.
turns.zh: 所以在 Salt Lake，你创办一家‘明星企业’（star business）的概率……

turns.en: Meaning the top 10% of revenue or employment is three times higher than if you grew up in Mississippi. And anecdotally, it's not entirely clear what's going on. There's the nickname, the Silicon Slopes, Salt Lake, but some of it might be that there's a large Mormon population and a common thing to do is to go on missionary work and bang on doors and have people tell you no, and you keep going, you get some resilience and grit and like there's no hard data and that's what's going on, but that seems kind of plausible to me.
turns.zh: 也就是收入或就业排在前 10% 的那种，是你在 Mississippi 长大的三倍。而且凭传闻来说，并不完全清楚到底怎么回事。有个绰号叫‘硅谷坡地’（Silicon Slopes），Salt Lake。但其中一部分可能是因为那儿有大量摩门教（Mormon）人口，而一件常做的事就是去做传教工作、敲人家的门、让人对你说‘不’，而你一直坚持，你就获得了一些韧性和毅力——虽然没有硬数据说就是这么回事，但在我看来这似乎挺说得通的。

turns.en: So that's, that's one thing.
turns.zh: 所以那是一件事。

turns.en: And you see it also for the children of business owners, they're way more likely to start a business themselves, even if you take all of the family firms out of the data. So it's like, you're not just inheriting, you know, your son is not inheriting the podcast, but just here's all about money all the time.
